title: Where the MLB gap lives: information, not calibration
headline_insight: In MLB the model's reliability is within 0.0066 Brier of the market's, but its resolution trails by 0.0235 -- the shortfall is missing information, not miscalibration.
what_it_means: A Murphy decomposition splits a Brier score into reliability (are the probabilities honest), resolution (do they separate winners from losers), and an irreducible uncertainty term. The MLB in-game model is almost as well-calibrated as the market (reliability differs by only +0.0066) but separates outcomes less sharply (resolution trails by -0.0235). That means re-scaling the probabilities cannot close the gap -- the market simply knows things the model does not.
how_to_read: Each reliability curve plots predicted probability against actual outcome frequency across 10 bins; the closer the curve hugs the diagonal, the more honest the numbers.
why_it_matters: It pinpoints the deficit as an information problem, not a calibration bug, so the right fix is better inputs (lineups, weather, late news), not recalibration.
caveat: Soccer's gap is far larger (model Brier 0.227887 vs market 0.142726) and its reconstructed Brier (0.293529) diverges from the direct Brier, a sign the 10-bin decomposition is coarse on the smaller n=9003 soccer corpus.
